brief: Coming off last weekend's AI regulation scare, market reaction this week was mild, framed by King Charles's Thursday meeting with AI leaders. Corporate commentary through Q2 earnings was unambiguous on AI, so the rates trajectory and by extension oil are judged more consequential near-term than AI headlines. Given the Fed's hawkish hike, Wilson adds an extra 25bps hike in October and does not see the November election as an impediment to a second hike, though it would be a bigger impediment to an initial hike. He argues now is the wrong time to be most fearful of higher rates: the move has largely happened, hikes are priced in excess of what he expects to realize, and inflation surprise risk skews lower because the extended Iranian conflict has not yet triggered an oil supply disruption large enough to push oil to new highs. Charts flag the 5yr return on a 10yr Treasury as the worst in over 120 years, interest expense hurting public finances more than private sector balance sheets, earnings growth driving more than 100% of stock returns, and European equities, still AI-nascent, positioned to benefit from lower energy prices and rising EU data-centre investment (PPC's AWS deal, following Google's deal with Fortum).
